records.name: Île-de-France
records.summary:
Île-de-France sits fractionally below the national 0.67, but the deviation is small because the negative and positive factors largely cancel for a traveller. On the negative side, the Paris agglomeration and urban units over 200,000 inhabitants concentrate 55% of anti-LGBT offences for 43% of the population—a rate of 9 per 100,000, more than double the rural 4 (2025 update: 54% for 43%, still 9 per 100,000 against the rural 4 and national 7). The 2025 Marche des Fiertés was mobilised under a heavy police frame; the self-declared "gay patriot" collective Eros sought to march with prefectural backing, Inter-LGBT threatened to cancel if it participated, and participants reported that "the Marche des fiertés is becoming a sensitive event." A visitor attending the Pride encounters organisational tension and a security apparatus that signals vulnerability even as it protects.

On the positive side, the 9-per-100k rate is heavily inflated by reporting propensity, community visibility, dedicated police liaison desks and the density of associations—all of which mean more incidents are recorded and responded to, not necessarily that a visitor is at greater risk; Paris alone records 22 per 100,000 but the official note cautions that offences there also involve non-residents (commuters and tourists). records.name: North Ossetia–Alania
records.summary:
North Ossetia–Alania is included in the North Caucasus zone that the UK Home Office CPIN (June 2025) singles out as the exception to its general finding of no state-persecution risk in Russia. Western travel advisories name the republic within the broader Caucasus don't-travel area. The enforcement logic is the same as neighbouring republics: family honour norms and informal security structures can produce violence, detention, or forced return without legal process.

No Chechnya-scale secret-prison infrastructure or explicit special-permission entry requirement is documented for North Ossetia specifically. Approximately 0.07 below national (0.12). Equal to Kabardino-Balkaria and Karachay-Cherkessia in the broader North Caucasus bloc. Well above the central-Russian oblasts, which inherit the national score with no sub-national deviation.

records.name: Moscow
records.summary:
Moscow is where the federal anti-LGBT framework is enforced most visibly. The Moscow Times' 2025 survey of persecution — headlined around “arrests, club raids and extremism charges” — records that the first person charged with creating an extremist organisation on LGBT grounds, Kotov, was arrested in Moscow in late December 2024; the paper reported Russia's first prison sentence under the LGBT-‘extremism’ designation in February 2025, an organising case following a ruling reported from Siberia in January 2025.

The severity of the federal law is uniform across the country, but enforcement intensity is not: Moscow concentrates the highest police density, the most active venue-level operations, and the bureaucratic touchpoints most likely to involve a foreign visitor — document verification, medical gatekeeping, registration procedures. For a trans visitor the practical result is a materially higher probability of encountering active enforcement of the same rules, and the country offers no protective institutional counterweight at any level.
